```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf

DATA_PATH = Path.home() / "Documents/GitHub/Data_Analytics/data"
assert DATA_PATH.exists(), f"Data directory not found: {DATA_PATH}"

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="talk")
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (10, 5)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 20)
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)

COLORS = {
    "observed": "#6B7280",
    "trend": "#D55E00",
    "seasonal": "#0072B2",
    "remainder": "#009E73",
    "outlier": "#CC3311",
    "missing": "#CC79A7",
    "imputed": "#E69F00",
}

def plot_series_matplotlib(df, *, x="ds", y="y", title="", xlabel="Time",
                           ylabel="Value", color="#0072B2", ax=None):
    """Stable plotting helper that does not depend on utilsforecast APIs."""
    if ax is None:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    else:
        fig = ax.figure
    ax.plot(df[x], df[y], color=color, linewidth=1.3)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel=xlabel, ylabel=ylabel)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig, ax
```

# Introduction

## Real time-series data are messy

A recorded series may contain:

- observations that are unusually large or small;
- values that are absent;
- zeros whose meaning is ambiguous;
- data-entry or sensor failures;
- genuine shocks and structural changes.

The first task is not automatic correction. It is **diagnosis**.

::: {.notes}
The source section states that real data often contain missing values, outlying observations, and other messy features. This lecture focuses only on that subsection.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Learning objectives

Students will be able to:

- distinguish an unusual observation from an error;
- visualize outliers in temporal context;
- use robust STL to isolate unusual remainders;
- apply and critique IQR-based detection rules;
- map missingness through time;
- distinguish missing values from structural zeros;
- compare deletion and imputation strategies;
- visualize uncertainty introduced by data cleaning;
- preserve an auditable trail of modifications.

::: {.notes}
The emphasis is visualization-led reasoning. Numerical rules support investigation but do not replace context.
:::

## A responsible workflow

```text
DETECT → VERIFY → CLASSIFY → DECIDE → MODIFY → COMPARE → DOCUMENT
```

Never begin with:

```text
DETECT → DELETE
```

::: {.notes}
The book warns that simply replacing outliers without thinking about why they occurred is dangerous because unusual values may contain useful information about the process.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

# Outliers

## What is an outlier?

An outlier is an observation that is very different from most observations in the time series.

An outlier may be:

- a recording or processing error;
- a valid but unusual event;
- evidence of model misspecification;
- evidence of a level shift or structural change.

::: {.notes}
The chapter explicitly states that outliers may be errors or may simply be unusual. The additional classifications are teaching categories for investigation.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Why time context matters

A value can appear ordinary marginally but be unusual for:

- its season;
- its neighboring observations;
- the current trend level;
- its day of week or quarter;
- the variance regime at that time.

> Outlier detection for time series should respect temporal structure.

::: {.notes}
This is a teaching recommendation. A global boxplot of the raw data may flag regular seasonal peaks rather than anomalies.
:::

## Adelaide Hills tourism data

```{python}
tourism_raw = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "tourism.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
tourism = (
    tourism_raw
    .loc[lambda x: (x["Region"] == "Adelaide Hills") &
                   (x["Purpose"] == "Visiting")]
    .assign(unique_id="trips")
    .reset_index(drop=True)
    [["unique_id", "ds", "y"]]
)
tourism.head()
```

::: {.notes}
This reproduces the series used in the source subsection: quarterly overnight trips to Adelaide Hills for the Visiting purpose.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Figure 13.9: Inspect the original series

```{python}
fig, ax = plot_series_matplotlib(
    tourism,
    title="Quarterly overnight trips to Adelaide Hills",
    xlabel="Quarter [1Q]",
    ylabel="Number of trips",
)
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The chapter identifies an apparently unusual observation in 2002 Q4. Ask students to describe the observation before labeling or replacing it.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Annotate suspected observations

```{python}
suspected_date = pd.Timestamp("2002-10-01")
suspected = tourism.loc[tourism["ds"] == suspected_date]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(tourism["ds"], tourism["y"], color=COLORS["observed"], linewidth=1.2)
ax.scatter(suspected["ds"], suspected["y"], color=COLORS["outlier"], s=90,
           zorder=3, label="Candidate: 2002 Q4")
ax.set(title="Candidate outlier shown in temporal context",
       xlabel="Quarter [1Q]", ylabel="Number of trips")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Use the label candidate outlier until the observation has been verified. Annotation makes the analytical focus visible without silently editing the data.
:::

## Why decompose before detecting?

Raw observations combine:

```math
y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t.
```

A seasonally high value may be normal. An unusual remainder is unusual **after accounting for estimated trend and seasonality**.

::: {.notes}
The chapter recommends STL decomposition as a useful way to reveal outliers in the remainder series.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Robust STL decomposition

```{python}
stl = STL(tourism["y"], period=4, robust=True)
stl_result = stl.fit()
dcmp = pd.DataFrame({
    "ds": tourism["ds"].to_numpy(),
    "data": tourism["y"].to_numpy(),
    "trend": stl_result.trend,
    "seasonal": stl_result.seasonal,
    "remainder": stl_result.resid,
})
dcmp.head()
```

::: {.notes}
The book implements robust STL through MSTL with one seasonal period. Here, statsmodels STL gives the corresponding single-season robust decomposition directly.
:::

## Figure 13.10: Components and remainder

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(11, 7))
for ax, column, label, color in zip(
    axes,
    ["data", "trend", "seasonal", "remainder"],
    ["Observed", "Trend", "Seasonal", "Remainder"],
    [COLORS["observed"], COLORS["trend"], COLORS["seasonal"], COLORS["remainder"]],
):
    ax.plot(dcmp["ds"], dcmp[column], color=color)
    ax.set_ylabel(label)
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Quarter")
fig.suptitle("Robust STL decomposition")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The source figure uses data, trend, and remainder panels. The seasonal panel is retained here because this is a visualization class and seasonal magnitude is diagnostically useful.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Remainder in time

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(dcmp["ds"], dcmp["remainder"], color=COLORS["remainder"])
ax.axhline(0, color="0.35", linewidth=1)
ax.scatter(suspected_date,
           dcmp.loc[dcmp["ds"] == suspected_date, "remainder"],
           color=COLORS["outlier"], s=90, zorder=3)
ax.set(title="Outliers should be judged against the remainder",
       xlabel="Quarter", ylabel="Remainder")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The remainder plot preserves time ordering, allowing detection of isolated spikes, clusters, and changes in variance.
:::

## IQR rule on the remainder

Let

```math
\operatorname{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1.
```

A general fence with multiplier $k$ is

```math
L=Q_1-k\operatorname{IQR},
\qquad
U=Q_3+k\operatorname{IQR}.
```

Flag observations for which $R_t<L$ or $R_t>U$.

::: {.notes}
The book discusses k equal to 1.5 and prefers a stricter k equal to 3 for this context.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Implement the chapter's 3-IQR rule

```{python}
q1 = dcmp["remainder"].quantile(.25)
q3 = dcmp["remainder"].quantile(.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
lower = q1 - 3 * iqr
upper = q3 + 3 * iqr
outliers = dcmp.loc[~dcmp["remainder"].between(lower, upper)].copy()
outliers
```

::: {.notes}
The source section reports that this rule identifies the suspected observation plus three additional observations in the example.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Visualize the fences and flags

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(dcmp["ds"], dcmp["remainder"], color=COLORS["remainder"], label="Remainder")
ax.axhline(lower, color=COLORS["outlier"], linestyle="--", label="3-IQR fences")
ax.axhline(upper, color=COLORS["outlier"], linestyle="--")
ax.scatter(outliers["ds"], outliers["remainder"], color=COLORS["outlier"],
           s=75, zorder=3, label="Flagged")
ax.set(title="Remainder-based candidate outliers",
       xlabel="Quarter", ylabel="Remainder")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Plotting the fences makes the rule auditable. The points are flags for investigation, not proof of error.
:::

## Boxplot of the remainder

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.boxplot(x=dcmp["remainder"], color="#56B4E9", whis=3, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Remainder boxplot with 3-IQR whisker rule",
       xlabel="Remainder")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The chapter recommends a boxplot of the remainder in more difficult cases. The horizontal time plot and boxplot answer complementary questions.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## A rule is not a diagnosis

Before replacing a flag, ask:

- Is the raw source correct?
- Did units or definitions change?
- Was there a one-off real event?
- Is the seasonal period correctly specified?
- Did the decomposition leave systematic structure?
- Is the value part of a level shift rather than an isolated outlier?

::: {.notes}
These are recommended diagnostic questions. The source warns against replacement without understanding why the observation occurred.
:::

## Isolated outlier versus level shift

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
idx = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=80, freq="D")
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
base = rng.normal(0, 1, 80)
isolated = base.copy(); isolated[40] += 8
level_shift = base.copy(); level_shift[40:] += 4
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharey=True)
axes[0].plot(idx, isolated); axes[0].set_title("Isolated observation")
axes[1].plot(idx, level_shift); axes[1].set_title("Persistent level shift")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
This is a teaching illustration. Replacing one point may be reasonable for a verified measurement error, but it would conceal a persistent regime change.
:::

# Missing Values

## Missing is not a value

A missing observation may mean:

- the event was not recorded;
- the device failed;
- the reporting process was delayed;
- the activity did not occur;
- the business was closed;
- the record is structurally inapplicable.

These meanings require different treatments.

::: {.notes}
The source distinguishes context-driven missingness, such as public-holiday closures, from essentially random recording failures.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Zero versus missing

```text
0       = observed absence or true zero quantity
NaN     = no usable observation is recorded
```

Never convert `NaN` to zero unless zero accurately represents the data-generating process.

::: {.notes}
The source gives a holiday-closure example where setting a missing value to zero may be reasonable when closure means zero sales, but the model must also account for holiday and post-holiday effects.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Missingness can be informative

The source example:

- a store is closed on a public holiday;
- sales are zero on the holiday;
- sales may increase on the following day;
- ignoring the mechanism can bias forecasts around the holiday.

No automated method can infer this business context on its own.

::: {.notes}
The chapter suggests setting holiday closure values to zero and using dummy variables for the holiday and the following day in an AutoARIMA model.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Create missing-value scenarios

```{python}
tourism_missing = tourism.copy()
tourism_missing.loc[[8, 9, 25], "y"] = np.nan
missing_dates = tourism_missing.loc[tourism_missing["y"].isna(), "ds"]
tourism_missing.head(12)
```

::: {.notes}
These missing observations are synthetic for teaching. Two are consecutive and one is isolated, allowing different visual and interpolation behavior to be discussed.
:::

## Show gaps honestly

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(tourism_missing["ds"], tourism_missing["y"], color=COLORS["observed"], marker="o")
for date in missing_dates:
    ax.axvline(date, color=COLORS["missing"], alpha=.35)
ax.set(title="Missing observations should appear as gaps",
       xlabel="Quarter", ylabel="Number of trips")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Do not connect across gaps without an explicit visual indication. Otherwise, the line suggests observed continuity.
:::

## Missingness map

```{python}
missing_indicator = tourism_missing["y"].isna().astype(int).to_numpy()[None, :]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 2.4))
sns.heatmap(missing_indicator, cmap=["#E5E7EB", COLORS["missing"]], cbar=False,
            xticklabels=tourism_missing["ds"].dt.strftime("%Y Q%q") if False else False,
            yticklabels=["y missing"], ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Temporal location of missing observations", xlabel="Observation order")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A missingness map reveals isolated gaps, blocks, and alignment across variables. The code intentionally uses observation order to avoid unsupported quarter formatting.
:::

## Count and locate missing observations

```{python}
missing_summary = pd.Series({
    "observations": len(tourism_missing),
    "missing": tourism_missing["y"].isna().sum(),
    "missing_share": tourism_missing["y"].isna().mean(),
    "first_missing": tourism_missing.loc[tourism_missing["y"].isna(), "ds"].min(),
    "last_missing": tourism_missing.loc[tourism_missing["y"].isna(), "ds"].max(),
})
missing_summary
```

::: {.notes}
A count alone is insufficient. Temporal location and run length determine whether a gap disrupts trend, seasonality, or the forecast origin.
:::

## Two options stated in the source

When a forecasting implementation does not accept missing observations:

1. use the section after the last missing value, if enough data remain;
2. replace missing values with estimates.

The choice depends on the context and forecasting purpose.

::: {.notes}
The source specifically states these two options in relation to StatsForecast not allowing missing values in the time-series data.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

# Imputation

## Interpolation is an estimate

Linear interpolation between observed endpoints $y_a$ and $y_b$ is

```math
\widehat y_t
=
y_a+
\frac{t-a}{b-a}(y_b-y_a),
\qquad a<t<b.
```

It assumes smooth movement between neighboring observations.

::: {.notes}
Interpolation creates estimated values, not recovered truths. Long gaps and seasonal series make the assumption less plausible.
:::

## Reproduce the source's interpolation approach

```{python}
outlier_dates = outliers["ds"]
tourism_cleaned = tourism.copy()
tourism_cleaned["was_replaced"] = tourism_cleaned["ds"].isin(outlier_dates)
tourism_cleaned["y_original"] = tourism_cleaned["y"]
tourism_cleaned.loc[tourism_cleaned["was_replaced"], "y"] = np.nan
tourism_cleaned["y"] = tourism_cleaned["y"].interpolate(method="linear")
tourism_cleaned.loc[tourism_cleaned["was_replaced"]].head()
```

::: {.notes}
The source replaces detected outlier values with missing values and then applies pandas interpolate. This version matches by date rather than value, avoiding accidental replacement of legitimate duplicate values.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Figure 13.11: Original and cleaned series

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(tourism_cleaned["ds"], tourism_cleaned["y_original"],
        color="0.75", label="Original")
ax.plot(tourism_cleaned["ds"], tourism_cleaned["y"],
        color="#0072B2", label="Cleaned")
replaced = tourism_cleaned.loc[tourism_cleaned["was_replaced"]]
ax.scatter(replaced["ds"], replaced["y"], color=COLORS["imputed"],
           s=80, zorder=3, label="Interpolated replacement")
ax.set(title="Quarterly overnight trips to Adelaide Hills",
       xlabel="Quarter [1Q]", ylabel="Number of trips")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Displaying original and cleaned values together preserves transparency. The source figure shows the cleaned series after interpolation.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Compare common imputation strategies

```{python}
comparison = tourism_missing[["ds", "y"]].copy()
comparison["linear"] = comparison["y"].interpolate("linear")
comparison["forward_fill"] = comparison["y"].ffill()
comparison["seasonal_lag4"] = comparison["y"].fillna(comparison["y"].shift(4))
comparison.loc[comparison["y"].isna()]
```

::: {.notes}
These are teaching alternatives, not methods prescribed by the source. Linear interpolation assumes local smoothness, forward fill assumes persistence, and seasonal lag substitution assumes seasonal repetition.
:::

## Visual comparison of imputations

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(comparison["ds"], comparison["y"], color="0.75", marker="o", label="Observed")
for column, color in zip(["linear", "forward_fill", "seasonal_lag4"],
                         ["#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"]):
    ax.plot(comparison["ds"], comparison[column], color=color, alpha=.85, label=column)
ax.set(title="Imputation methods encode different assumptions",
       xlabel="Quarter", ylabel="Number of trips")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The disagreement between methods is a visual representation of imputation uncertainty. Do not select a method solely because it produces the smoothest line.
:::

## Gap length matters

```{python}
missing_mask = tourism_missing["y"].isna()
run_id = missing_mask.ne(missing_mask.shift()).cumsum()
missing_runs = (
    tourism_missing.assign(missing=missing_mask, run_id=run_id)
    .loc[lambda x: x["missing"]]
    .groupby("run_id")
    .agg(start=("ds", "min"), end=("ds", "max"), length=("missing", "size"))
)
missing_runs
```

::: {.notes}
An isolated gap and a long missing block should not automatically receive the same treatment. Long gaps weaken local interpolation and may span structural changes.
:::

## Do not overwrite the raw data

Keep at least:

- original value;
- cleaned or imputed value;
- modification flag;
- reason for modification;
- method used;
- parameters or window;
- analyst review status.

::: {.notes}
This is a recommended governance pattern. It supports reproducibility and auditability.
:::

## An auditable cleaning table

```{python}
audit = tourism_cleaned.loc[tourism_cleaned["was_replaced"],
                            ["ds", "y_original", "y"]].rename(
    columns={"y": "replacement"}
)
audit["reason"] = "3-IQR flag on robust STL remainder"
audit["method"] = "linear interpolation"
audit
```

::: {.notes}
The detection rule is recorded separately from the replacement method. A flag does not establish that an observation is erroneous.
:::

# Visual Diagnostics After Cleaning

## Compare decomposition before and after

```{python}
original_fit = STL(tourism["y"], period=4, robust=True).fit()
clean_fit = STL(tourism_cleaned["y"], period=4, robust=True).fit()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(11, 6))
axes[0].plot(tourism["ds"], original_fit.trend, label="Original trend", color="0.5")
axes[0].plot(tourism["ds"], clean_fit.trend, label="Cleaned trend", color=COLORS["trend"])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Trend"); axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
axes[1].plot(tourism["ds"], original_fit.resid, label="Original remainder", color="0.5")
axes[1].plot(tourism["ds"], clean_fit.resid, label="Cleaned remainder", color=COLORS["remainder"])
axes[1].set(xlabel="Quarter", ylabel="Remainder"); axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
fig.suptitle("Cleaning changes estimated components")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Cleaning is not neutral. It can change the trend, seasonal component, remainder, and subsequent forecasts. Compare before and after explicitly.
:::

## Remainder ACF before and after

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
plot_acf(original_fit.resid, lags=16, zero=False, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Original remainder ACF")
plot_acf(clean_fit.resid, lags=16, zero=False, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Cleaned remainder ACF")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A cleaner-looking ACF is not proof that replacement was correct. It only shows how the modeling residual structure changed.
:::

## Visual honesty checklist

- show gaps rather than silently connecting them;
- use a distinct marker for imputed values;
- retain the original series for comparison;
- disclose the detection rule;
- disclose the replacement method;
- avoid calling flags confirmed errors;
- report how many observations were modified;
- inspect whether cleaning changes substantive conclusions.

::: {.notes}
This checklist translates the source warning into visualization practice.
:::

# Decision Framework

## Outlier decision tree

```text
FLAGGED OBSERVATION
        ↓
VERIFY SOURCE AND UNITS
        ↓
ERROR? ── YES → REPLACE / CORRECT + AUDIT
  │
  NO
  ↓
RECURRING OR FORECAST-RELEVANT EVENT?
  ├─ YES → RETAIN + MODEL EVENT
  └─ NO  → RETAIN OR ROBUSTLY DOWNWEIGHT,
           BASED ON FORECAST PURPOSE
```

::: {.notes}
The source says replacement is more defensible if the value is genuinely erroneous or if the event will not occur during the forecast period.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

## Missing-value decision tree

```text
MISSING OBSERVATION
        ↓
WHAT DOES MISSING MEAN?
  ├─ TRUE ZERO / CLOSURE → ENCODE ZERO + EVENT VARIABLES
  ├─ RANDOM RECORDING FAILURE → ESTIMATE IF NEEDED
  ├─ STRUCTURAL NON-APPLICABILITY → RETAIN AS MISSING
  └─ UNKNOWN → INVESTIGATE BEFORE IMPUTING
```

::: {.notes}
The source emphasizes that treatment depends on forecasting context and that automated methods cannot infer contextual effects such as public holidays.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/13-practical.html#sec-missing-outliers
:::

# Practice

## Classroom exercise

Using the Adelaide Hills series:

1. plot the raw series and annotate 2002 Q4;
2. perform robust STL with period 4;
3. calculate 1.5-IQR and 3-IQR remainder fences;
4. compare the flagged sets;
5. investigate whether flags form isolated points or clusters;
6. replace only one selected candidate by interpolation;
7. compare trend and remainder before and after;
8. create an audit table;
9. explain why the chosen treatment is defensible;
10. state what evidence remains unavailable.

::: {.notes}
Assessment should reward reasoning, transparency, and visual comparison rather than maximizing the number of detected outliers.
:::

## Missingness experiment

Create three versions of the series:

- one isolated missing quarter;
- four consecutive missing quarters;
- one missing seasonal peak every year.

For each version:

- visualize the pattern of missingness;
- compare linear, forward-fill, and seasonal-lag imputation;
- explain which strategy is least implausible;
- identify possible forecast bias.

::: {.notes}
This extension illustrates that the temporal mechanism and gap pattern matter more than a universal imputation rule.
:::

## Assessment rubric

| Dimension | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Temporal reasoning | seasonality and trend are removed before flagging |
| Visualization | candidates, gaps, and replacements are visible |
| Context | error, event, zero, and missing are distinguished |
| Method | detection and replacement procedures are explicit |
| Sensitivity | alternative thresholds or imputations are compared |
| Transparency | original values and audit flags are retained |
| Interpretation | cleaning consequences are assessed, not hidden |

::: {.notes}
A strong submission treats cleaning as a model choice with consequences.
:::

# Key Takeaways

## Main conclusions

1. An outlier can be an error or a genuine event.
2. Time-series outliers should be judged relative to temporal structure.
3. Robust STL can isolate unusual values in the remainder.
4. IQR fences produce candidates, not confirmed errors.
5. Missing values and zeros are not interchangeable.
6. Missingness mechanisms can affect forecast bias.
7. Interpolation is an assumption-based estimate.
8. Different imputations can produce different stories.
9. Cleaning can alter trends, seasonality, remainders, and forecasts.
10. Every modification should remain visible and auditable.

::: {.notes}
End by asking students whether a smoother series is necessarily a more truthful series. The correct answer is no.
:::

## Final checklist

- [ ] Was the original series plotted first?
- [ ] Was trend and seasonality considered before flagging?
- [ ] Are flags described as candidates?
- [ ] Was the source or event context investigated?
- [ ] Is missing distinguished from zero?
- [ ] Are missing runs and locations shown?
- [ ] Is the imputation assumption explicit?
- [ ] Are imputed points visually distinct?
- [ ] Are original and cleaned results compared?
- [ ] Is there an audit table?

::: {.notes}
This checklist is suitable for forecasting reports, dashboards, and production data-quality workflows.
:::
